title: Starting my First Machine Learning Project — And my First Blog Post in Forever
description: Starting my First Machine Learning Project — And my First Blog Post in Forever A return to scripting. Embarking on my first machine learning project feels like coming full circle in my coding …
author: Ammar
content_chunks: Embarking on my first machine learning project feels like coming full circle in my coding journey. I’ve always been drawn to the intersection of technology and creativity, and now, I’m diving into the world of machine learning with a newfound passion. Join me as I document my experiences, starting with this blog post. My first venture into writing any sort of machine-read instructions was in elementary school, writing BAT scripts which would repeatedly open and close the classroom PC’s CD/DVD drives. Next I experimented with proxies to unblock gaming sites and access Tor, before eventually stumbling onto early malware development

forums (this was ~2014, I was ~16). This was the golden age of banking trojans, formgrabbers, rootkits, and MITB and MITM attacks. We all learned to write from the same old Russian IRC bot source-codes. Lean, C code was the name of the game, and knowing both the documented and undocumented functions of the Windows kernel and OS processes was a constantly honed skill. The state-of-the art malware and crypters were polymorphic, which, funnily enough, can almost be thought of as a precursor to any use of AI in malware and in my eyes was one of the first signs

that neural-network style computing concepts were nearing readiness for mass use, by non-mathematicians. The nights I spent in my room up all night, in such a specific pose my brother drew a sketch of me coding which I still keep to this day, stumbling for hours to get over whatever current hurdle I was facing in the project I had undertook, are burned into my brain. The process of research in general is one thing which LLMs such as ChatGPT, and their democratization, have drastically changed (arguably making it a more powerful and efficient process) but that is discussion is

outside the scope of this post. And what do I know: I can hardly imagine people of my parents generation, before the internet, who everything they know was read from a book they looked for and picked up, physically. The difference in effort and involvement in learning is simply striking and I don’t know what to make of it in terms of a normative judgement. In the time since high school, I have stepped back and broadened both my interests and skills. I will admit for a couple of years this did not mean much more than getting into trouble

with my friends, but throughout school courses, work, and natural social interaction, I have fostered a true interest in the following non-cybercrime related areas: market psychology / marketing, financial markets, infrastructure and population growth, governments and power structures, sustainable food production, history and war, fishing, hiking, camping, cooking, and anything to do with evolution, biology, or the two. Quantum computing and AI were the trends to be on the lookout for over the next decades. Smart-glasses projects were being rumored and beta’d, as well as iffy human chat-bots. Here we are, 8–10 years later. Python was gaining in popularity even

back in the 2010s, as were powerful scripting languages in general. Thus I familiarized myself with it at the time but did not put in much practice. Well I am glad I at least did that, because a whole lot of other people have been busy making great libraries for us to enjoy (The democratic and open-source nature of the community pushes the language forward, as is true of the scientific community in general. From what I can see and what its worth, R has been a greatly developed language which I also intend to get to know, but for

right now I will stick to my Python). And luckily for us, even more in the work of bringing AI to the masses has been done than I could have imagined. Teams of people behind projects such as scitkit-learn, PyTorch, and fast.ai, to name a few, have a provided excellent architecture and tools allowing the proliferation of all variety of machine and deep learning models. Thus naturally, my last main interest which has formed in my time since malware research, is the application of these, essentially advanced statistics techniques, to real world problems. AKA machine and deep learning. That interest

has been enough to spur me to begin documenting my journey again, for my own sake and for record. I was re-introduced to statistics and regression a couple of years ago in a university class, and was inspired to begin learning about web-scraping and public data sources of all types. You can see on my GitHub a number of projects relating to scraping and parsing various data sources started at the time. Anyways, the other month, I finally got around to diving into how exactly to implement my own deep learning solution, and what was all the hype about data

analysis really about? So I have embarked on fast.ai’s Practical Deep Learning for Coders course, both via the video lessons by Jeremy Howard, and the notebooks posted to the course’s GitHub. As it currently stands, I am in the middle of lesson 3 / chapter 4, and have up until this point created a simple pothole recognition model using a fastai vision learner and a restnet18 model trained to images I pulled from Bing. I have also experimented with the Titanic Kaggle competition corresponding to lesson 3. However, as I let the derivative math of stochastic gradient descent of chapter

4 glue itself together and really solidify again (its been a few years), I figured I would embark on my own simple project, outside the direct scope of the course. Mr. Howard, if I remember correctly, even encourages it as a way to practically learn, via your own curiosity. That has given me the idea for my own first self-driven machine learning project: analyzing SEC filings. If you are unfamiliar, the SEC’s EDGAR database houses an extensive record of filings from publicly traded companies, which hold financial and other information (It is an awesome data source, as are many large

government regulators and bodies, for some pretty interesting information. Poke around). Particularly, I have chosen to begin with NLP of S-1 filings (prospectus filings, made when a company goes public on the stock market). I plan to use both LDA and NMF techniques for topic analysis to identify trends in prospectus language, and topics, over time. Sentiment analysis and other NLP techniques will follow, as well as analysis of other filing types. As of today, I have began writing a jupyter notebook which aims to help scrape the summary and risk factor sections of S-1 filings, with a configurable timeframe.

This is basically a streamlined adaptation of code I wrote a couple of years ago for parsing 10-Q and 10-K filing text sections (in foresight of this exact type of project). It currently relies on the BeautifulSoup python library to parse HTML style filings, and I am currently experimenting to make this parsing more reliable. I suppose here is where we face the first decision of whether to involve machine learning: Do I bother trying to train a model to locate and extract the target filing sections for me or do I try to develop a framework to do it

‘manually’ and keep the involvement of machine learning down the road, not as something to be tried along every step? I ask somewhat sarcastically, but to illustrate what I think will become a more valid and general question: at what point is it appropriate to bring in the big dogs? For now, I say too soon. For now I will try to optimize my manual section-grabbing code. Perhaps, if unsuccessful, I will resort to employing a model specifically for this purpose. In its code’s current state, it relies on a hyperlinked table of contents to exist in order to reference

and find the text of the target sections’. While essentially all modern filings include HTML formatted data, not all have hyperlinked tables of contents, and these are not caught by my parse. Relevant to other financial facts, it may be worth it to further investigate the iXBRL formatting which filers now adhere to, but it seems for some text sections it is still lacking in usefulness. To be truly as compatible as possible, it would be best to have methods to also parse a filing with either a non-hyperlinked table of contents of no table of contents at all (and

filings from prior to HTML formatting norms). Perhaps margins or other text styling will prove worth relying on. I have been warned many places along the way that obtaining and engineering useful data is more time consuming than actually applying models and analyzing it will be, as is how things generally go. When I return with some topic results, I will also attempt to give a non-computer scientist explanation of how a basic neural network works and is trained via SGD, and perhaps an update on what I have read about LDA and NMF maths and implementations. My future posts
shouldn’t be so long winded or all over the place; I just wanted to give some context to my journey and provide somewhat of a background piece. Figured I had to start somewhere.

author: Amruta

This technology is used by computers to understand, analyze, manipulate, and interpret human languages. NLP algorithms, leveraged by data scientists and machine learning professionals, are widely used everywhere in areas like Gmail spam, any search, games, and many more. These algorithms employ techniques such as neural networks to process and interpret text, enabling tasks like sentiment analysis, document classification, and information retrieval. Not only that, today we have build complex deep learning architectures

title: Natural Language Processing (NLP)  -  Introduction
description: A Friendly Introduction to Natural Language Processing (NLP) to know what is NLP ? why it is so important ? and what are some of it's applications ?
author: Mounir Boulwafa
content_chunks: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is “a branch of artificial intelligence that helps computers understand, interpret and manipulate human language. NLP draws from many disciplines, including computer science and computational linguistics, in its pursuit to fill the gap between human communication and computer understanding.” Also we can define NLP as “a convergence of artificial intelligence and computational linguistics which handles interactions between machines and natural languages of humans in which computers are entailed to analyze, understand, alter or generate natural language.” And according to Wikipedia, Natural language processing (NLP) is “a subfield of linguistics, computer science, information engineering, and artificial intelligence

concerned with the interactions between computers and human (natural) languages, in particular how to program computers to process and analyze large amounts of natural language data.” NLP is about making computers understand how humans speak and communicate with each other in order to help the computers to engage in communication using natural human language in many forms, including but not limited to speech and writing. We talk to each other in a number of different ways, whether it’s through different grammatical structures or the regional idioms we use, so it’s essential that NLP is in place so that this gap

in communication can be bridged. Apart from personal assistants like Siri, Alexa and Google Assistant, some other applications of NLP include sentiment analysis, speech recognition and so on, so let’s talk about some of it’s applications : Machine translation (MT) refers to the automatic translation of a segment of text from one language to another. Humans may use MT to help them render text and speech into another language, or the MT software may operate without human intervention. MT tools are often used to translate vast amounts of information involving millions of words that could not possibly be translated the

traditional way. The quality of MT output can vary considerably; MT systems require “training” in the desired domain and language pair to increase quality. We are all familiar with Google Assistant, Apple’s Siri, Amazon’s Alexa, and Microsoft’s Cortana, and so on. all those virtual assistants AI technologies are built based on Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Natural Language Understanding (NLU), a procedure of converting speech into words, sounds, and ideas. So speech recognition is simply the ability of a software to recognize speech. Anything that a person says, in a language of their choice, must be recognized by the software.

Speech recognition technology can be used to perform an action based on the instructions defined by the human. The human needs to train the speech recognition system by storing speech patterns and vocabulary of their language into the system. By doing so, they can essentially train the system to understand them when they speak. Sentiment Analysis (also known as opinion mining or emotion AI) is an interesting type of data mining that measures the inclination of people’s opinions. The task of this analysis is to identify subjective information in the text. Sentiment analysis helps to check whether customers are satisfied

with goods or services. Classical polls have long faded into the background. Even those who want to support brands or political candidates are not always ready to spend time filling out questionnaires. However, people willingly share their opinions on social networks. The search for negative texts and the identification of the main complaints significantly helps to change concepts, improve products and advertising, as well as reduce the level of dissatisfaction. In turn, explicit positive reviews increase ratings and demand. Text classification also known as text tagging or text categorization is the process of assigning a set of predefined categories to

free-text or categorizing text into organized groups. By using Natural Language Processing (NLP), text classifiers can automatically analyze text and then assign a set of pre-defined tags or categories based on its content. Text classification is becoming an increasingly important part of businesses as it allows to easily get insights from data and automate business processes. There are many interesting applications for text classification such as spam detection, email routing and sentiment analysis etc… Chatbots are applications that interact with users, usually over text, via websites or integrated into other platforms to ensure that customers get answers to their questions

or find what they’re looking for, in real time. Chatbots provide a conversational experience between the customer and the company without all of the extra steps of actually ringing up the customer service department. The importance of NLP for a chatbot application is in making the customer feel understood in real time. Much like a human assistant, Natural Language Processing is what allows chatbots to understand and to dialogue with customers : it can ask questions and understand answers, identifying all the relevant information in the conversation in order to automate and effectively empower the customer assistance process. Automatic Summarization

or Text summarization is the technique for generating a concise, meaningful and precise summary of voluminous texts (such as books, news articles, blog posts, research papers, emails, and tweets) while focusing on the sections that convey useful information, and without losing the overall meaning.Automatic text summarization aims to transform lengthy documents into shortened versions, something which could be difficult and costly to undertake if done manually and its is one of the most challenging and interesting problems in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). A spell checker or spell corrector is a technique which identifies the incorrect or misspelled

words in a block of text and replaces them with the best possible combination of correct words. For find incorrect word firstly system checks the word in the dictionary. If the word is finding in the database then it assume to be correct word and if it is not present in the database then system assume this word incorrect and perform the required process to generate best possible combination of correct word. Spell checking is one of the applications of Natural Language Processing that impacts billions of users daily, and most text editors (like Microsoft Word for example) or even

search engines let users check if their text contains spelling mistakes. Generally Natural Language Processing can be split into two parts the Understanding part (NLU) and the Generation part (NLG) : NLU or Natural Language Understanding is a subset of NLP that is responsible for the semantic parsing and analysis, entities extracting…etc. NLU tries to structure the input data to understand the meaning behind written text. For example after having the speech recognition software convert speech into text, The NLU system comes into the picture to decipher its meaning. It is quite possible that the same text has various meanings,

or different words have the same meaning, or that the meaning changes with the context. Knowing the rules and structure of the language, understanding the text without ambiguity are some of the challenges faced by NLU systems. NLG or Natural Language Generation is the step when the machine tries to transform the structured (from NLU) data into human-readable language, so NLG does exactly the opposite of NLU. Given the data, it analyzes it and generates narratives in conversational language. It goes way beyond template based systems, having been configured with the domain knowledge and experience of a human expert to

produce well-researched, accurate output within seconds. Narratives can be generated for people across all hierarchical levels in an organization, in multiple languages. Natural Language Generation has made its presence felt in various domains ranging from banking and financial services to media, healthcare, and education. It is here to stay to help businesses improvise their processes and tread faster on the path of advancement! author: Gabriela Bitencourt-Ferreira, Walter Filgueira de Azevedo
content_chunks: Molegro Virtual Docker is a protein-ligand docking simulation program that allows us to carry out docking simulations in a fully integrated computational package. MVD has been successfully applied to hundreds of different proteins, with docking performance similar to other docking programs such as AutoDock4 and AutoDock Vina. The program MVD has four search algorithms and four native scoring functions. Considering that we may have water molecules or not in the docking simulations, we have a total of 32 docking protocols.

The integration of the programs SAnDReS ( https://github.com/azevedolab/sandres ) and MVD opens the possibility to carry out a detailed statistical analysis of docking results, which adds to the native capabilities of the program MVD. In this chapter, we describe a tutorial to carry out docking simulations with MVD and how to perform a statistical analysis of the docking results with the program SAnDReS. To illustrate the integration of both programs, we describe the redocking simulation focused the cyclin-dependent kinase 2
